title: Niche positioning on a small site
excerpt: A small site should name its buyer and its offer on the first screen. A specific position is easier to prove than a claim that you do everything.
alt: Skyscrapers photographed from street level against a pale sky, a scale a small site should not try to imitate when it says who it is for.
caption: Street-level towers. A small site should name who it is for. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Where should the niche appear?
faqs.answer: In the title and on the first screen, in a sentence a stranger can repeat. Name the buyer and the offer. A poetic line can remain if the next sentence does that job. Project captions should be able to say the same focus in their own words.

faqs.question: Should a small site have a page for every industry?
faqs.answer: Wait until a buyer type is real, with different questions and proof you can show. Pages that swap a city or an industry into the homepage blur the position. A home, an offer, proof, and a way to start a conversation are enough while you are still proving the niche.

faqs.question: How do I know the position is too broad?
faqs.answer: Read the site for ten seconds and try to say who it is for and what they make. If you can only say that they do design, the focus is still private. Then check the first project. If it would disappoint someone who believed the title, change the title or change what leads.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A niche marketing website gets clearer, and easier to find, when it says who it is for in the title and on the first screen. A page that claims every audience sounds like no audience, and it competes with firms that have spent years earning the broad words.

That choice should be visible. One buyer. One offer. Proof that matches both. The rest of the menu can wait until those three are unmistakable.

## Say who it is for before you say what you do

The first screen has two jobs: what this is, and how to talk to a person. Niche positioning adds a third that makes the first two possible. Name the buyer. "Product design and web development for founders" is a position. "We craft digital experiences for brands worldwide" is a fog. The first can be checked against the work. The second can be claimed by anyone with a homepage.

Put the buyer in the title element and in the opening sentence. [Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive, concise text, and it warns against boilerplate that makes every page sound the same. A specific title is how a small site avoids that trap. "Hanabi | Product Design & Web Development Studio" tells a stranger the category and leaves room for the page to say founders, websites, brand systems, and product interfaces. A poetic line can stay as the brand H1 if the next sentence answers who and what.

Do this on the inner pages too. A service page that says "websites" and never says for whom will collect the wrong comparisons. A project page that names the kind of client, a heritage craft brand, a shop, a community sports club, teaches the niche by example.

## A specific offer beats a full catalog

Head terms such as "web design agency" are crowded with directories and firms that have had years to collect links. Chasing them produces a homepage that lists every service and ranks for none of them. The queries worth writing toward are the ones a founder types while deciding: a marketing site, a landing page, a brand system, an ecommerce rebuild, a product interface.

Choose the offer you can show. Hanabi's public work includes an ecommerce move for Down the Cove, an editorial site for Thomas Bewick, a community sports site for Ballarat Box Sports, a calm brand site for Wabisabi, and product interfaces such as Got Next, Leadly, and Trade Moai. That set supports a position: a small studio that designs and builds, with a visible craft standard, for founders and small teams. It does not support "we are the right partner for every industry and every budget." Saying the smaller thing is how the larger thing stays believable later.

[Google's helpful-content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether your site has a primary purpose or focus. A niche is that focus written in public. The same guidance warns against entering a topic mainly because you expect traffic, without real experience. Position yourself where you have done the work. If you have not shipped a complex product, do not lead with enterprise platform language. If your best proof is a careful brand site, lead with that and let the product work arrive when it is real.

Write down the projects you will turn away. A good niche includes a no. Engagements that need a large agency, or builds that are only a plugin install, are better served elsewhere. That sentence is more quotable than a list of adjectives, and it saves both sides a call that should not happen.

## Proof that matches the claim

The first screen makes a promise. The work section keeps it. If you say you build calm brand sites, the first project should feel calm. If you say you design product interfaces, at least one frame should be a product, with a decision a reader can see. Mixing every style you have ever tried, with equal weight, undoes the sentence at the top.

Captions should name the project and the view. "Dashboard" is weaker than "Leadly, a product interface organized around the next action." You do not need a metric to make the proof specific. You need the constraint and the object.

Keep the voice inside the same niche. A site that looks quiet and reads like a hype reel is two positions at once. Pick three sentences you are willing to say, and three you will not. Apply them to the headline, the button, and the project intro. Hanabi's line worth repeating is clarity over complexity: quality, clean code, a process that can change, speed, and plain communication. That is a niche of manner, and it should show up in the work, not only in a manifesto.

## Pages that can wait

A small site does not need a page per industry, city, or synonym. Those pages repeat the homepage with a noun swapped in, and they blur the position you just worked to make sharp. Wait until a buyer type is real, with proof and a different set of questions, before you give it a URL.

Until then, a tight set is enough: home, the offer, proof, a way to start a conversation, and writing that answers the searches around that offer. Each of those pages should be able to say the niche in its own first paragraph without copying the homepage word for word. The homepage states it. The service page shows what it means for a website or a product. The project page shows it in a single engagement.

Postpone the "we also do" row until the primary offer is obvious. Extra skills, a bot, a design system, a frontend revamp, can sit in a quieter band. They should not lead. A visitor who came for a marketing site should not have to reconstruct your focus from a grid of twelve capabilities.

## How to check the position

Read the site the way a stranger will, on a phone, for ten seconds. You should be able to finish three sentences: this is for these people, they make this kind of thing, here is how to talk to them. If you finish with "they seem to do design," the niche is still in your head.

Then search your own title against the work. Would the first project disappoint the person who believed the title? If yes, change the title or change which project leads. The position is a promise you keep on the next screen, not a slogan you hope the work will grow into.

When you are ready to give the niche a full structure, the companion piece is [the pages a seed-stage site actually needs](/blog/pages-a-seed-stage-site-needs). A position without a small set of pages is still a sentence. The pages are how a buyer moves from that sentence to a conversation.

[Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) are built around that kind of focus: websites, brand systems, and product interfaces for founders, designed and built by the same studio. The niche is the offer, stated narrowly enough that the right person recognizes themselves.
